title: Multi-region priority queue threshold leakage and guardrail implementation
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Summary: During an upstream traffic surge on 2026-03-08 we observed an emergent failure mode where per-region priority queues slowly leaked higher-priority tokens into secondary-region routing windows, leading to silent amplification of cross-region load and an SLO miss for 95th and 99th tail latency across several customers. The incident was not a single hard failover — it was a slow bleed-through due to mismatched queue quota enforcement and circuit hysteresis settings across regions, compounded by an edge routing policy that favored capacity-aware spillover without backpressure. This ticket captures the postmortem findings and the prioritized guardrail implementation plan.
timeline:
2026-03-08 09:34 UTC — First elevated error-rate alert on eu-west-1 tail latency.
2026-03-08 09:42 UTC — Traffic spike identified originating from large internal batch job; primary region (us-west-2) nearing saturation.
2026-03-08 09:46 UTC — Automated spillover moved 18% of requests to eu-west-1; priority queue quotas in eu-west-1 began to climb.
2026-03-08 09:51 UTC — We observed rising 99th latencies and queue-timeouts in eu-west-1; circuit breakers did not trip due to conservative hysteresis.
2026-03-08 10:05 UTC — Manual partial rollbacks and emergency shedding rules rolled out to reduce cross-region affinity.
2026-03-08 10:32 UTC — SLO window (7d P95/P99) registered breach for multiple customers; oncall declared incident.
2026-03-08 11:10 UTC — Mitigations stabilized traffic; degradation resolved by 11:45 UTC.
2026-03-09 to 2026-03-12 — Root cause analysis, reproducer construction, and initial PRs created for guardrails and observability enhancements.
impact: Customer-facing: ~42 customers experienced increased tail latency; 6 enterprise customers reported degraded request success rate during the 30m peak. SLO effects: P95 increased from baseline 120ms to 420ms in eu-west-1 for affected routes; P99 spiked to >1.8s. Internal: incident page and oncall rotation consumed ~14 engineer-hours. No data loss. Financial: low immediate chargeback, but potential for SLA credits if recurring.
root_cause: Three factors combined: (1) Priority queue quota counters were only enforced locally and synced with eventual consistency; this allowed a transient oversubscription when spillover increased traffic faster than quota reconciliation. (2) Circuit breaker hysteresis and open-window goals were tuned to avoid flapping, which prevented timely tripping under sustained bleed-through. (3) Edge spillover policy did not apply per-tenant priority caps when routing to secondary regions, so high-priority tenants could push volume into a region already at capacity for other tenants. Observability gaps: missing per-tenant queue heatmaps and inadequate tags on trace spans that would show cross-region queue migration paths.
mitigations: Immediate: applied emergency per-tenant rate caps at the edge, lowered spillover weight to 5%, and tightened circuit breaker hysteresis thresholds for the affected routes. Created temporary fallout rule to prefer local degradation over cross-region spillover for P0 tenants. Longer-term: implement hard per-region priority queue quotas with synchronous admission control, add faster circuit tripping for sustained queue-growth patterns, and enrich traces with queue-owner and routing-decision metadata.
follow_up_summary: We will treat this as a reliability pattern: 'priority leakage' — where logical priority semantics leak under spillover. The work is split into observability, runtime enforcement, routing policy changes, and testing (chaos + replay). The highest priority items are: (A) synchronous per-region admission controls to prevent quota leakage, (B) circuit hysteresis redesign to support gradient tripping, and (C) observability additions to detect early leakage and surface tenant-level heatmaps.
